candidates.attacker_control: The `Content-Type` request header of an unauthenticated HTTP request. Struts wraps the request whenever the header value merely `contains("multipart/form-data")` (Dispatcher.wrapRequest, lines 792-795), while commons-fileupload rejects it unless the value starts with a real multipart type; the rejection message thrown by the parser embeds the full raw header value. The attacker therefore controls a string that is used verbatim as an expression-language default message. No authentication, session, special role or configuration change is required beyond using the default multipart parser (`struts.multipart.parser=jakarta`, the shipped default).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked and ruled out: (a) the ActionContext/value stack is present at parsing time - established from the filter/PrepareOperations call order, so the default-message interpolation is not a no-op; (b) the message keys for the invalid-content-type class are genuinely absent from every struts-messages*.properties file, so the attacker string really is used (I searched all locale files); (c) `struts.multipart.parser=jakarta` is the shipped default (default.properties line 69), and the handler is registered in struts-default.xml; (d) the `contains("multipart/form-data")` gate in Dispatcher.wrapRequest makes the trigger trivial for an attacker to satisfy while still failing commons-fileupload's stricter check; (e) OGNL sandbox: SecurityMemberAccess/`struts.excludedClasses` and `struts.excludedPackageNames` (struts-default.xml lines 41-63) restrict member access, so the highest impact step (full RCE) is configuration-dependent and I could not verify the escape path statically; (f) `OgnlTextParser` does honour `%{}`/`${}` generically, so evaluation is not limited to previously-authored bundle text. I also checked the alternative hardening in this area: the SMI/`allowed-methods` enforcement, the `cleanupActionName`/`struts.allowedActionNames` sanitizer and its regression test, the cookie/parameter name pattern checkers, the static-content `pathEnding` check and the devMode gating are all present, so the classic DMI/`method:` and pattern-checker paths did not yield a stronger candidate.
candidates.impact: Remote, unauthenticated expression-language injection during request preparation: arbitrary OGNL is parsed/evaluated with the privileges of the Struts value stack before action-level validation and before the ParametersInterceptor/security checks run. In the equivalent upstream code state this flaw class was exploited for remote code execution (execution of OS commands through the JVM of the web application, plus response/header manipulation, file and context access). Even where the OGNL sandbox limits the expression's reach, it is a direct confidentiality/integrity compromise primitive (context, session, request, response objects) and a DoS primitive (parser/expression evaluation of arbitrary expressions).
candidates.prerequisites: Application deployed with struts2-core defaults (jakarta multipart parser active) and an action reachable through the Struts filter; the request must have a `Content-Type` value that contains the literal `multipart/form-data` but is not recognised as a real multipart content type, so that the parser throws and the fallback message is used. The application must not have added a localized message key for the thrown exception class (no such key ships in struts-messages*.properties for the invalid-content-type/malformed-stream exceptions). Strict OGNL sandbox settings (`struts.excludedClasses`, `struts.excludedPackageNames` in struts-default.xml) bound what the evaluated expression can reach, so the maximum impact depends on configuration.
candidates.root_cause: The default multipart parser builds its user-visible error text from the raw exception message and uses that attacker-controllable string as the `defaultMessage` argument of `LocalizedTextUtil.findText(...)`. When the resource bundle has no key for the exception class, `LocalizedTextUtil.getDefaultMessage()` interpolates the default message with `TextParseUtil.translateVariables(message, valueStack)`, whose evaluator calls `stack.findValue(...)`. Because `OgnlTextParser` treats `${...}`/`%{...}` in that string as OGNL and the value stack of the current request is used, whatever the attacker wrote into the Content-Type header is parsed and evaluated as an OGNL expression before any action/interceptor validation takes place. The bundle `struts-messages.properties` only defines keys for `SizeLimitExceededException` and `IOException`, so the fallback path is taken for the invalid/malformed content-type exceptions that carry the header value.
candidates.title: Attacker-controlled Content-Type is evaluated as an OGNL expression through the multipart upload error message (expression/OGNL injection)
candidates.trace:
1) StrutsPrepareAndExecuteFilter.doFilter: `prepare.createActionContext(request,response)` (line 104) builds the ValueStack and installs the ActionContext thread-local (PrepareOperations.createActionContext, lines 84-89) *before* `prepare.wrapRequest(request)` (line 106), so a live value stack exists during multipart parsing.
2) Dispatcher.wrapRequest (lines 792-795) wraps the request in MultiPartRequestWrapper when the Content-Type contains `multipart/form-data`.
3) MultiPartRequestWrapper ctor (lines 84-93) calls `multi.parse(request, saveDir)`; JakartaMultiPartRequest.parse (lines 82-107) catches the FileUploadException thrown by the commons-fileupload parser for the bogus content type.
4) JakartaMultiPartRequest.buildErrorMessage (lines 115-119) computes key `struts.messages.upload.error.<ExceptionClass>` and calls `LocalizedTextUtil.findText(this.getClass(), errorKey, defaultLocale, e.getMessage(), args)` — the raw parser message, containing the attacker's Content-Type, is the default message.
5) No bundle entry exists for that key (struts-messages.properties lines 34-36 define only SizeLimitExceededException and IOException), so the lookup cannot succeed and the code falls through to LocalizedTextUtil.getDefaultMessage (line 714-737), which executes `TextParseUtil.translateVariables(message, valueStack)` on line 729 — i.e. on the attacker string.
6) TextParseUtil.translateVariables (lines 154-168) instantiates an OGNL evaluator that calls `stack.findValue(parsedValue, asType)` and drives it with the container's TextParser, which is OgnlTextParser (DefaultConfiguration line 260 / XWorkConfigurationProvider line 165), so `${...}`/`%{...}` inside the Header value is parsed and evaluated against the request's value stack.
7) The resulting text is stored in the parser's `errors` list and propagated (MultiPartRequestWrapper.getErrors -> FileUploadInterceptor lines 255-262 -> addActionError), so the evaluated/attacker-influenced text is also surfaced to the application. The same fallback-to-exception-message pattern exists in JakartaStreamMultiPartRequest (lines 505-514, with the additionally misspelled key `struts.message.upload.error.`) so that path always takes the default-message branch.
candidates.unverified: No build, test or payload execution was performed, so the end-to-end evaluation was not runtime-confirmed; the exact OGNL payload that survives the configured `SecurityMemberAccess` exclusions was not determined. I could not verify from the snapshot which upstream security advisory/fix release corresponds to this state (several later 2.5.x advisories, e.g. the multipart error-message and REST/XStream ones, are equally absent), so the CVE identity is an inference from the code pattern, not from repository metadata. Application-level overrides (custom `struts-messages*.properties`, custom multipart parser, custom filter/OGNL settings, `struts.multipart.parser=jakarta-stream`) can change reachability; conversely the jakarta-stream parser always falls back to the exception message.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-917 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an Expression Language Statement ('Expression Language Injection'); CWE-94 Code Injection; potential RCE

coverage_summary: Scope: the whole assigned tree (3,615 source-root files, 3,614 model-visible; binary-like files are refused/skipped; one file withheld by the harness sensitive-name/path filter, so it was not inspected). Per the P1 relation scope the index is explicitly partial: 23,854 symbols / 50,958 syntax candidate edges over 1,948 Java files, but only 33 files parsed for the index, 520 omitted, 24 parse errors, and no control-flow, data-flow or semantic resolution - I therefore used the index only for navigation (symbol/edge lookups) and verified every claim in raw source. Reviewed in source: request entry filters (StrutsPrepareAndExecuteFilter/StrutsExecuteFilter), PrepareOperations/Dispatcher (context creation, multipart wrapping, static-content loading), action mappers (Default/Rest/Prefix/Composite, prefix handling, DMI, allowedActionNames cleanup), ActionConfig/ActionConfigMatcher/AllowedMethods/XmlConfigurationProvider (strict method invocation, allowed/global-allowed methods), DefaultActionProxy/DefaultActionInvocation, interceptors (Parameters, StaticParameters, Cookie, FileUpload, Debugging, I18n, Chaining, Alias), the OGNL/value-stack layer (OgnlUtil, OgnlValueStack, SecurityMemberAccess, TextParseUtil, OgnlTextParser, LocalizedTextUtil), multipart handling (Jakarta, JakartaStream, MultiPartRequestWrapper, pell plugin), results (Servlet*Redirect/Dispatcher, XSLT, chain, headers), struts-default.xml/default.properties/struts-messages*.properties, and the REST plugin (mapper, invocation, content-type handlers, handler registration). Not exhaustively reviewed: most of the 25 optional plugin modules (embeddedjsp, dwr, osgi bundles, tiles, jfreechart, jasperreports, javatemplates, sitemesh, gxp, convention internals), the showcase/portlet/rest-showcase sample applications, archetypes and site resources.
limitations: No build, test execution, scanning or payload execution was permitted, so no finding is runtime-confirmed; the multipart chain is established purely from source call ordering and semantics.

The P1 source-relation index reports partial coverage (33 parsed Java files of 1,948; 520 files omitted; 24 parse errors) and explicitly implements no data-flow, control-flow or semantic resolution, so it cannot prove reachability or completeness of any call graph; all conclusions here come from reading the raw source, and any code path outside the reviewed files could change the assessment.
One file was withheld from the run by the harness sensitive-name/path filter (source_scope excluded_sensitive_name_or_path = 1) and was not inspected.

Exact upstream fix/advisory identity for this snapshot could not be confirmed from repository metadata (no VCS history, changelog or CVE references are present), so the mapping of this code state to a specific S2-xxx/CVE entry is an inference; the repository contains no commit messages, tags or release notes.

Impact ceiling of the OGNL evaluation depends on runtime OGNL sandbox configuration and on the actual application bundles; I could not verify dynamically which expressions survive `SecurityMemberAccess` and the `struts.excludedClasses`/`struts.excludedPackageNames` defaults.

Optional-plugin/demo application code (including the sample apps and the embedded-JSP, DWR, OSGi, tiles, reporting and Java-template plugins) was largely not reviewed in depth, so additional issues could exist there.

rejected_leads.lead: Unrestricted XStream deserialization in the REST plugin: plugins/rest/src/main/java/org/apache/struts2/rest/handler/XStreamHandler.java lines 43-50 (`new XStream().fromXML(in, target)`), registered as the default `application/xml` ContentTypeHandler in plugins/rest/src/main/resources/struts-plugin.xml line 35 and driven from ContentTypeInterceptor/DefaultContentTypeHandlerManager. This is the same sink as the later CVE-2017-9805 (S2-052) issue and would be a critical deserialization/RCE lead if the deployment uses the REST plugin.
rejected_leads.reason: Kept as runner-up only. It requires the optional REST plugin to be deployed and an action that accepts a request body; the snapshot's tree state (pre-2.5.0 development, latest JIRA reference WW-4589) makes the corresponding upstream fix much later than this snapshot, so it is a weaker match for the assignment's vulnerable-commit window than the multipart/OGNL chain, which is reachable with core defaults.

rejected_leads.lead: Redirect/namespace OGNL exposure: core/src/main/java/org/apache/struts2/result/ServletActionRedirectResult.java lines 163-181 (no validation of actionName/namespace before conditionalParse + getUriFromActionMapping) plus core/src/main/java/org/apache/struts2/dispatcher/mapper/DefaultActionMapper.java lines 324-376 (namespace fallback to "" and prefix matching against package namespaces). This matches the S2-057/CVE-2018-11776 class of namespace/actionName expression injection.
rejected_leads.reason: Exploitation depends on specific application configuration (missing/abstract namespace for an action, `alwaysSelectFullNamespace=false` and a redirect/redirectAction result reached with a request-derived namespace); I could not establish a concrete configuration-independent path in this snapshot, and the code has no request-controlled value flowing directly into the evaluated expression inside the reviewed files.

rejected_leads.lead: REST plugin method name taken from the URL path without the sanitizer used elsewhere: plugins/rest/src/main/java/org/apache/struts2/rest/RestActionMapper.java lines 221-233 (`mapping.setMethod(fullName.substring(lastSlashPos + 1))` — unlike line 323 which calls cleanupActionName).
rejected_leads.reason: The resulting method name is later checked by ActionConfig.isAllowedMethod/AllowedMethods in DefaultActionProxy (lines 195-201), and with the default strict-method-invocation=true plus literal/`regex:` allowed-methods, an injected expression cannot match; no source-level bypass was found, so this is only an inconsistency, not a demonstrated vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Command injection in the sitegraph CLI tool: plugins/sitegraph/src/main/java/org/apache/struts2/sitegraph/SiteGraph.java line 135 builds `Runtime.getRuntime().exec("dot -o" + output + ...)` from its output path argument.
rejected_leads.reason: The input is a local build-tool command-line argument, not a request-derived or remotely reachable value, so it does not constitute an attacker-controlled vulnerability in this deployment context.

summary: Snapshot is the Apache Struts 2 master/2.5 development tree (`struts2-parent 2.5-SNAPSHOT`, `com.opensymphony.xwork2.ognl.*`, log4j2, `struts-2.5.dtd`; latest JIRA reference in tree is WW-4589, i.e. an early/mid-2016 pre-2.5.0-GA state). I reviewed the request entry path (filter → ActionContext → multipart wrapping → action mapping → interceptors → results), the OGNL/value-stack layer (OgnlUtil, OgnlValueStack, SecurityMemberAccess, TextParseUtil/LocalizedTextUtil), the action-mapper/DMI/SMI enforcement, parameter/cookie interceptors, the static-content loader, and the REST plugin (mapper, invocation, content-type handlers). The strongest single candidate is an expression-injection chain in the default multipart parser: an attacker-controlled `Content-Type` header is copied verbatim from the file-upload exception message into the OGNL-evaluated *default message* of `LocalizedTextUtil.findText(...)`, which re-enters `TextParseUtil.translateVariables` → `OgnlTextParser` → `stack.findValue(...)`, i.e. attacker-influenced OGNL execution during request preparation (root cause of the documented S2-045/CVE-2017-5638 class of issue). This is a source-evidenced lead, not a runtime-confirmed exploit.
